title: Peer Memory (Person + Department)
markdown:
An external, peer-keyed memory layer gives the Executive durable cross-channel recall, sitting on top of Honcho via `openexecutive.memory.honcho_client`. The `HONCHO_ENABLED` env var gates it; when false every entry point short-circuits with `outcome=disabled` and behavior matches the pre-Honcho posture.

### Two scopes

- **Per-person**, keyed by `Person.id` — a user chatting from Discord, Telegram, email, or web is one peer card, so facts shared in any channel surface in the others. Each entry point resolves the caller to a `Person.id` (channel-ID lookups for adapters; `x-caller-email` for web).
- **Per-department**, keyed by `department_<slug>` — each department accumulates an institutional voice from dept-scoped decisions, advice, committee outcomes, and dept-bound specialist turns.

### Flow

`prefetch` runs once per turn and injects a `<peer_memory>` block into the user turn (empty on timeout or error). `HONCHO_PREFETCH_MODE` picks how the block is produced. `representation` (the default) reads the person's peer card and the derived conclusions most relevant to the inbound message straight from Honcho (`peer.context(search_query=…)`, `HONCHO_PREFETCH_MAX_CONCLUSIONS` of them, default 20): a GET with no LLM behind it, about 100 ms self-hosted. The block keeps whole lines only, up to a size cap (a line that does not fit is dropped, never cut), strips control characters and defangs a literal closing tag, since conclusions derive from text anyone who can email the Executive wrote. A person Honcho knows nothing about yet yields no block and an `empty` audit outcome. `dialectic` asks Honcho's chat endpoint with the message as the question and injects the synthesized prose (an LLM call, seconds), where `reasoning_level` trades latency for depth. The mode applies to every per-person prefetch, committee turns included. Only `prefetch_department` (one dialectic question per consulted specialist that maps to a department, yielding `<department_memory>`) and the `ask_about_person` tool always use the chat endpoint: they are deliberate questions off the inline path, the split Honcho's own guidance draws between `context()` for per-turn grounding and `chat()` for reasoned answers. After the response, `sync_turn` and `sync_department_turn` persist the exchange as fire-and-forget background tasks that never block the user. The Executive's reply is written under an `executive` peer resolved with `observe_me=false`: the person's representation sees both sides of the exchange, but Honcho no longer derives a representation of the Executive itself, which nothing read and which is where a person's words were occasionally misattributed to the Executive. Both record the person's words only. Honcho derives facts about a person from everything posted under their peer, so a turn whose prompt carries text the person did not write passes `memory_text` to `Executive.chat` / `stream_chat` / `stream_chat_with_committee`, and that — not the prompt — is what both syncs post: an inbound email records its subject, the sender's new text and the attachment filenames (never the "You have an inbound email" framing, the headers with the Executive's own address in `To:`, the `[POLICY]` notice or the quoted chain, which held the Executive's own earlier email and taught Honcho that the sender *was* the Executive); a web upload records the typed text and filenames, not the extracted document text; a briefing handoff records a short line of what the user asked ("Asked to discuss the flagged artifact …"), not the Executive's card body it seeds. Without `memory_text` the prompt is recorded, as before. The `<outbound_reply_context>` block that inbound hydration prepends for the LLM turn is also stripped before the message is posted, and from the prefetch query, so the Executive's own DM is never learned as something the person said.

### What it knows, on Pulse

The Pulse page's Memory section has a **People** tab beside Decisions, Initiatives and Advice, backed by `GET /memories/people` (`people_overview`). It is read-only and costs no LLM call: one listing of the workspace's peers, then, for each peer that matches a rostered person by id, one page of that person's self-conclusions (newest first, `?recent=` of them, plus the total) and one card read with the identity lines the roster already supplies stripped out. Peers are matched, never created — `peer(id)` is a get-or-create POST, and a page you merely open must not mint peers for people who have never talked — and the `executive` and `department_*` peers and archived people are skipped. The listing runs under one clock (the SDK walks every page, bounded only per request otherwise) and each person is then read under the unscaled prefetch budget, at most eight at a time because these reads share the client with the live chat prefetch; one person's failure or timeout marks only that entry (`error`) and the others still render. The header and the tab share one in-flight request per page load. The header's Memories tile adds the conclusion total to the three episodic counts (its hint says how many are peer notes) without waiting on the read, and the tab hides itself when peer memory is disabled. Peers are matched only by an id spelled exactly as OE writes it, once per person, so a stray or repeated peer skips rather than fails or double-counts; within the newest page the conclusions are ordered by instant here (not by the rendered timestamp, which is not chronological across offsets) rather than trusting the server's order. Card elements and conclusions are split on physical lines before the scrub, so an identity claim on the second line of one element is caught too. Every line passes the same control-character and closing-tag scrub as the `<peer_memory>` block, since the text was derived from what people wrote. One `peer_memory` audit row per call, `op=overview`.

### Prefetch budget

In representation mode the prefetch is a single read with no LLM behind it: it runs on `HONCHO_PREFETCH_TIMEOUT_S` unscaled and `reasoning_level` is ignored. The rest of this section is the dialectic mode.

`HONCHO_PREFETCH_TIMEOUT_S` is the knob for the **fast per-turn path** and is used unscaled there. The two per-turn callers pick different levels on purpose: `stream_chat` awaits the prefetch inline before the first streamed byte and defaults to `minimal`, the cheapest level, after `low` was measured hitting the ~5 s tail for peers with large representations; the chat route runs the prefetch inside the same gather as knowledge and episodic retrieval, so its `low` adds no dead air of its own and buys a fuller answer. Only the deliberate levels scale off it — `medium` 4x, `high` 5x, `max` 6x — capped by an absolute ceiling and never taken below the configured base. At the default 3s base that is 12s for `medium` with `high`/`max` at the 15s ceiling; at a 10s base every deliberate level *is* the ceiling. The multipliers only differentiate below it — the ceiling is the binding constraint at realistic bases, by design.

Honcho's dialectic latency scales steeply with the level (roughly 2s at `low` against 8s at `medium`), so a single flat budget made the deeper levels unreachable: every `medium` call — the committee path — timed out and the turn silently ran with no peer memory at all, which is strictly worse than having asked for `low`. `medium` gets more headroom than its measurement alone implies because the budget spans `peer()` plus `chat()`, and a budget set at the mean still times out on half the calls.

The fast levels stay unscaled for two reasons: `prefetch` is awaited inline before the first streamed byte, so multiplying the base there would add dead air to every ordinary turn; and a multiplier above 1.0 flattens every level onto the ceiling once the base approaches it, which would make the operator's knob stop distinguishing the two paths. Each prefetch audit row records the `timeout_s` it ran under.

The SDK client's HTTP timeout is an **outer** bound, kept strictly greater than every *per-call* budget; the aggregate ceilings on whole passes are deliberately not folded in, since it applies per request and would otherwise hand every unbudgeted call a bound several times too long. Because it is no longer a tight bound, all three fire-and-forget bodies (person sync, department sync, department note) — whose individual calls are not separately budgeted — carry their own aggregate ceiling, as does the session listing in the workspace purge.

### Peer identity

Peers are keyed by `Person.id`, so the only identity signal Honcho gets from the key alone is a bare integer — and its dreaming agent concludes that the number *is* the person's name (observed in production as a card reading `IDENTITY: Name: 1`). Because cards are injected into the dialectic system prompt on every `chat()`, that error propagates into every later answer about that person. So both sync paths seed each person peer's card from the roster, for the sender, the department-turn originator, and co-present peers alike.

The card carries the **name only** — email and role would export roster PII to a third-party memory service, including for people who were merely cc'd, and neither is needed to fix the defect. `set_card` replaces the whole card, so only `IDENTITY:` lines are swapped and the deriver's own `ATTRIBUTE:` / `RELATIONSHIP:` lines survive; the existing card is split on physical lines first, since one list element may itself span lines and hide an identity claim on its second.

Roster values are attacker-reachable — `upsert_person` is a chat tool an inbound email sender can reach — so a value is NFKC-normalised, stripped of control and format characters, whitespace-flattened, length-capped, and then held to an **allow-list** of letters, combining marks, digits and a small punctuation set, with the colon lookalikes the category allow-list would otherwise admit **stripped out** — taken from Unicode's confusables data (everything it maps to `:`), not from character names, since U+A4FD `ꓽ` is a Lisu *tone letter* whose name never says colon. They are stripped rather than grounds for refusing the value, because the visarga is the nominative ending in formal Devanagari and Gujarati names: refusing would leave those people never seeded, while stripping keeps the name as its stem form and still lets no colon shape reach the card. Modifier letters as a class stay allowed (々 in 佐々木, ー in ジョーンズ, ʻ in Hawaiʻi). A deny-list of structure tokens is not enough here: the consumer is an LLM system prompt rather than a parser, so `ATTRIBUTE :`, a fullwidth colon and a homoglyph all read the same to the model while defeating a literal match. The allow-list refuses every colon variant, which is what card structure depends on — checked by an exhaustive test over every Unicode codepoint whose name contains COLON plus an explicit test of the confusables the names miss. It does **not** stop a value that is merely persuasive prose — OE already embeds `full_name` in its own system prompt, so that exposure is pre-existing rather than introduced here.

Seeding runs *after* the message write and *outside* the sync ceiling, and is audited as its own `seed_identity` row (`ok` only when no peer's attempt failed; `error` when any did, with the `failed` count on the row; `timeout` when the pass or the roster read hit its ceiling; `empty` when there was nobody to seed) — so the sync row is a pure record of the persist, emitted the instant the write lands, and a slow card round trip can neither delay nor replace it. It is bounded per peer *and* per pass, and is best-effort. It is memoized per `(workspace, person)` on the facts sent with a recheck interval — a rename re-seeds immediately, and because the deriver keeps re-deriving identity from the peer id, a one-shot memo would let `IDENTITY: Name: 1` come back unnoticed. A failed attempt is memoized separately and briefly — including every peer a pass-ceiling cut-off left in flight or unreached — so a degraded card endpoint is probed once per interval rather than once per peer per turn.

### Cross-pollination & isolation

When a person turn touches a department, the dept peer joins the person's session as a co-present peer — the hybrid peer graph that lets later queries synthesize across both timelines, with synthesis depth degrading at greater peer-graph distance. Demo fixtures run in a sacrificial `openexec-fixture-<name>` workspace so demo turns never pollute real peer cards. Every wrapper call emits a `peer_memory` audit row (`op` + `outcome`) into the per-turn flow at `/audit/session/{id}`.
